summary: Children aged 6-7 learn to compare and sort a mixed collection of 2-D shapes, 3-D solids and everyday objects by geometric PROPERTIES — number of sides, number/type of faces, flat vs curved surfaces, number of vertices — and to articulate the criterion used. The procedural goal is a consistent, property-based sort: choose one attribute, apply it to every item, then re-sort the SAME collection a different way. This builds on knowing the properties and pushes children off the van Hiele visual level, where they group by overall look, colour or size. Best taught with real shapes to handle, 'is / is not' two-set sorting, and 'guess my rule' games.
misconceptions: Sorts by a non-defining feature — colour, size or overall look — rather than a geometric property.
Groups shapes by holistic resemblance ('these look the same') and cannot state a single consistent rule, letting the rule drift mid-sort.
Miscounts sides, faces or vertices — losing track of where counting started — so shapes end up in the wrong group.
Can sort one way but cannot re-sort the same collection by a different property, or cannot infer the rule of a set sorted by someone else.

activities.title: Sort a real tray two ways on an 'is / is not' rule
steps: Take a physical, mixed tray of handleable 2-D shapes, 3-D solids and everyday objects.

Choose ONE geometric property as the rule (e.g. 'has a curved surface / has no curved surface') and place every item into one of two sorting hoops or a labelled two-set frame. Check that the rule makes sense for every item in the tray: a flat 2-D shape such as a circle has a curved side (edge) but no curved surface, so either agree how 2-D shapes are judged or pick a rule that fits both 2-D and 3-D items (e.g. 'has a curved edge or surface / has none').
Say the rule aloud ('all of these have a curved surface') and check: does EVERY shape in this group follow my rule?
Now scatter the SAME shapes and re-sort them by a different property (e.g. 'has a triangular face / has no triangular face'); notice which shapes move to a different hoop and why.
activities.insight: A sort rests on one geometric property held constant and applied to every item; the same collection can be grouped validly in more than one way depending on which property you choose.

activities.title: Guess my rule
steps: Look at a set someone else has already sorted into two groups, with the rule hidden.
Infer and state the geometric property that was used to make the two groups.
Continue the sort by placing a few more shapes into the correct group, keeping the rule constant.
Then set your own 'guess my rule' challenge for a partner.
activities.insight: Making the hidden criterion explicit forces attention onto defining properties and shows that a good sort rests on one rule every member satisfies.

activities.title: Count faces, edges and vertices accurately before sorting
steps: Hold a real solid and mark each face, edge or vertex with a wipe-clean pen as you count it, so you count each one exactly once.
Record the count, then use it as the sorting rule (e.g. 'sort solids by number of faces' or 'six or more vertices / fewer than six vertices').
Recount a solid a second way and check you get the same total; if not, find where you lost track.
Place each solid in the correct group based on the verified count.
activities.insight: A count-based sort is only as reliable as the count; marking each feature once prevents losing track and keeps the sort consistent.

activities.title: Inspect 3-D solids for flat vs curved surfaces
steps: Pick up and rotate each solid to inspect every surface, feeling and looking for flat versus curved surfaces.
Sort the solids into 'has a curved surface / has no curved surface' based on what you found.
Explain for a tricky solid (e.g. a cylinder) which surfaces are flat and which are curved.
activities.insight: Rotating a solid to inspect all its surfaces reveals properties that a single view hides, supporting an accurate flat-vs-curved sort.

checkQuestion: Give the child a mixed tray of 2-D shapes and 3-D solids. Set the task and watch: 'Sort these into two groups so that everything in a group shares something. When you are done, tell me your rule.' Then: 'Now sort the same shapes a completely different way.' Finally, hand them a set you have already sorted and say: 'What was my rule?'
checkAnswer: Sorts by a stated geometric property — e.g. 2-D shapes by number of sides, or 3-D solids by flat-vs-curved faces or number of faces/vertices — applies it consistently to every shape, articulates the rule ('these all have a curved surface'), re-sorts the same collection by a different property, and infers the property behind a set sorted by someone else.
